<reason>Both sides were strong, but B built the cleaner path to victory. B framed the motion narrowly, grounded consent-as-floor in plausible analogies (wiretap provider exceptions, medical records, orphan-works copyright), and answered both pressure questions completely: unreachable parties via de-identification plus categorical statutory exceptions, and lawful possession via the purpose/beneficiary distinction ("a hospital holds your records and still cannot sell them"). B then turned A's best examples — smart replies resolve into "platforms can ask their own users," and the de-identification attack was caught on both horns. The decisive comparative survived to the end: A's alternative regime is firm-run self-assessment with unverifiable after-the-fact remedies ("consent minus the person"; "a promise made by the taker after the taking"), and A never specified who adjudicates it. A landed real hits — breach symmetry, the redesign concession, grandfathering/"amnesty with a moat" — but suffered two clipped turns (an execution cost), left its overbreadth point underexploited in the closing, and mirrored B's "who chooses, and when" frame less persuasively than B deployed it. B's closing crystallized the ex ante individual act versus ex post firm promise contrast without new material.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2: the A2 answer deployed the provider-exception/purpose-beneficiary distinction plus the hospital-records analogy to neutralize A's spam-scanning attack on "the taking is the injury," then B4.6 converted A's entire alternative into "consent minus the person: paperwork filed by the party with the incentive to take" — a reframe A never escaped.</best_rebuttal>
